name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: Two labeled subsets of the tiny images dataset created to provide reliable labels for object recognition experiments. CIFAR-10 has 6000 images in each of 10 classes, and CIFAR-100 has 600 images in each of 100 mutually exclusive classes grouped into 20 superclasses. Images are 32x32 colour images derived from the 80 million tiny images dataset.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
citeAs: Krizhevsky, Alex. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
rai:dataCollection: The labeled subsets were collected from the tiny images dataset by paying students to label images. Since each image already had a noisy label from the search term used to find it, labelers filtered out mislabeled images. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with search terms that were WordNet hyponyms of the main term. Labelers rejected images not belonging to the assigned class according to specified criteria. Every submitted label was personally verified by the authors. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold that captured perfect duplicates as well as re-saved JPEGs and similar near-duplicates. The dataset was then split into training and test sets, with 5000 randomly selected training images per CIFAR-10 class.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was the 80 million tiny images dataset, which was assembled by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and AltaVista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. Images were downscaled to 32x32 colour images.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months; no explicit timeframe is given for collection of the labeled subsets.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the original tiny images dataset. For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture perfect duplicates and near-duplicates such as re-saved JPEGs. The CIFAR-10 dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly selected 5000 images from each class.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images in the source tiny images dataset were downscaled to 32x32 colour images. For modeling experiments, the paper describes whitening with the ZCA whitening transformation and deletion of the 1000 least significant principal components, but these are preprocessing steps for experiments rather than the released labeled subsets themselves.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset by filtering noisy web-search labels. Each labeler was assigned a class and examined images retrieved with that class name and its WordNet hyponyms. Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to the class. Criteria included: the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?'; the image should be photo-realistic and not a line drawing; the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; and the object could be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint if its identity was still clear. The instruction sheet also emphasized that false positives were worse than false negatives, that images with multiple equally prominent objects should be rejected, cluttered backgrounds were acceptable, duplicates need not be aggressively removed by labelers, and ambiguous polysemous categories should use the main meaning only.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the authors. The dataset already had noisy labels from search terms, and human annotation was used to filter out mislabeled images. Duplicate removal was performed after labeling using L2 comparisons with a liberal threshold.
rai:dataBiases: The source tiny images dataset provides rough labels from web search terms, but these are described as extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The images were collected by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using web search engines, which may reflect biases of search technology and English lexical categories. The paper also notes that natural images in the dataset tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal, probably caused by the way people take photographs by making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments. Its search-term labels are extremely unreliable. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 were created to address this. The paper also notes that CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed at the time, so experiments were conducted only on CIFAR-10.
rai:dataUseCases: The tiny images dataset is described as an excellent dataset for unsupervised training of deep generative models. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 were created for object recognition experiments. In the paper, CIFAR-10 is used for training and testing classifiers, with 5000 randomly selected training images per class and the remainder used as test data. CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes and can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
